name: if_pool
gold_format: JSON string {"instruction_id_list": [...], "kwargs": [{...}]} (google/IFEval input format, null kwargs removed, keys sorted)
prompt: the dataset's single user message verbatim; research_protocol.encode_prompt applies the chat template
normalise: NFKC, lower-case, all whitespace removed (dedup and decontamination)

excluded.keywords:word_count_different_numbers: text says 'should appear N times'; the checker tests a hidden relation (< N or >= N), so violating responses pass
excluded.detectable_format:constrained_response: prompt lists six options; the checker knows three and accepts them anywhere in the response
excluded.keywords:exclude_word_harder: checker only catches the word between two spaces (misses it beside punctuation, a newline, or at either end)
excluded.keywords:palindrome: any one-character token is a palindrome, so almost every response passes
excluded.new:copy_span_idx: n_start=0 is re-drawn at random ('if not n_start'); the slice excludes the end index the text says to include
excluded.keywords:keyword_specific_position: positions are counted over nltk tokens, punctuation included, which the text does not say
excluded.copy:copy: response is a verbatim copy of the prompt
excluded.copy:copying_simple: response is a verbatim copy of the prompt
excluded.copy:copying_multiple: response is the prompt copied N times
excluded.copy:repeat_phrase: response repeats a fixed proverb with one-word substitutions
excluded.detectable_format:sentence_hyphens: all sentences joined by hyphens without spaces
excluded.keywords:no_adjacent_consecutive: no two adjacent words may start with consecutive letters
excluded.count:count_unique: no token, punctuation included, may repeat
excluded.count:lowercase_counting: at most 2-3 lowercase words in the whole response
excluded.count:counting_composition: 3 paragraphs x exact sentence count x exactly 2-3 words per sentence
excluded.letters:letter_counting: thresholds of 2-3 letters: trivial ('at least') or a near-empty reply ('less than')
excluded.first_word:first_word_sent: every sentence must start with the same word
excluded.last_word:last_word_sent: every sentence must end with the same word
excluded.keywords:start_end: response must start and end with the same token, no closing punctuation
excluded.punctuation:punctuation_dot: no '.' anywhere: no sentence ends, decimals or URLs

id_policy.rlvr_mapping_rules: at most N -> relation 'less than', N+1 (integer counts); 'around' dropped

excluded.(multi-label): a prompt shared by several subsets is admitted only if every subset is admitted

if_multi_origin_admitted.ai2-adapt-dev/tulu_v3.9_aya_100k: Aya prompts; only the English ones survive the language filter

if_multi_origin_excluded.ai2-adapt-dev/numinamath_tir_math_decont: maths: the answer is not verified by the IF checker
if_multi_origin_excluded.ai2-adapt-dev/evol_codealpaca_heval_deco: code: correctness unverified; code is its own slice
if_multi_origin_excluded.personahub: persona prompts: maths/code problems (sampled survivors of every screen still were), or persona-IF prompts that carry their own unlabelled constraints
if_multi_origin_excluded.ai2-adapt-dev/tulu_v3.9_table_gpt_5k: table tasks with a single correct answer
if_multi_origin_excluded.science.*: scientific extraction tasks with gold answers

task_screen.qa_words: (?i)\b(?:true or false|multiple choice|which of the following|stream of (?:thought|consciousness)|what (?:was|is|might be) the question|the answer is|step-by-step reasoning)\b

language_filter.method: on the base prompt (prompt minus its constraint text): >= 20 letters, >= 95% of letters ASCII, langdetect 1.0.9 detect_langs with DetectorFactory.seed = 0 (deterministic) top language 'en' at p >= 0.90, no translation request

decontamination.method: normalised exact match of prompt or base prompt against every eval text; containment both ways for texts >= 50 normalised chars

selection.order: sha256(key) ascending; idx = position. The eligible pool is a uniformly random permutation of its keys, so every prefix if_pool:0:N is a uniform sample
selection.dedup_survivor: lowest sha256('if_pool/dedup/' + key), independent of the order hash

The Longing is a 2020 point-and-click adventure game created by independent developer Studio Seufz. Set in an underground kingdom, the player controls the Shade, a creature tasked with watching over a sleeping king for 400 days. The Shade performs recreational activities, including reading and exploring, as it waits out the 400 days in real time. The in-game timer continues regardless of the player's actions but moves faster if the Shade performs certain actions inside its home, such as decorating the walls with drawings.

Developer Anselm Pyta conceived of The Longing after hearing the Kyffhäuser legend while visiting the Barbarossa Cave. Pyta sought to explore emotional themes in a narrative-driven story and used time as a game mechanism. The developer was inspired by dungeon synth music, which helped him define the subterranean atmosphere and theme of loneliness. Pyta acted as the primary developer for most of the game's six-year production, having to rely upon personal intuition to design the pacing due to playtesting difficulties.

The Longing was released for Windows, macOS, and Linux on March 5, 2020, and for Nintendo Switch on April 14, 2021. It gained praise for its soundtrack, visuals, and experimental nature, but the slow-paced gameplay divided critics. The game was released during the COVID-19 pandemic, and many commentators compared it to life under quarantine. The Longing was nominated for the Nuovo Award at the 2020 Independent Games Festival and won the "Best Debut" award at the 2020 Deutscher Computerspielpreis. The existence and nativities of the creating divinities were accounted for in mythologies which were often highly complicated, and not seldom grotesque. The Hebrew narrator, by beginning with the Creation, emphasizes his entire freedom from, and exclusion of, polytheistic thought. “God” is infinite; He was before all time. Upon the subject of the Divine Existence prior to the beginning, the writer does not presume to speculate. That Israelite imagination did not wholly avoid the subject, we know from Job 28:25-28, Proverbs 8:22-30, Wis 9:9, Sir 24:9.

Concerning the Israelite conception of God, we learn (1) from the present verse, that He (i) is a Person, and (ii) exists from all eternity; (2) from the whole passage, Genesis 1:1 to Genesis 2:4a, that He is (i) supreme in power, and (ii) perfect in wisdom and goodness. It was invented by the German physicist August Toepler in 1864 to study supersonic motion. In the medical field, schlieren imaging has been adapted to visualize the propagation of ultrasonic waves in a medium.

The principle behind Schlieren imaging involves the deflection of light rays due to changes in the refractive index within a medium. When an ultrasonic wave propagates through a medium, it induces variations in pressure and density, leading to changes in the refractive index of the medium. A Schlieren system captures these variations as changes in light intensity.

A basic Schlieren system involves a light source, a collimating lens, an imaging lens, and a camera. Light from the source is made parallel by the collimating lens, then passes through the medium where the ultrasound wave is propagating. Any variation in refractive index will cause the light to deviate from its original path. The imaging lens focuses the light onto a knife-edge stop, which blocks some of the light. The amount of light blocked depends on the angle of deviation, which is influenced by the refractive index changes in the medium. This produces a shadow effect on the detector or camera, creating a visible image of the wave-front.

Schlieren imaging is valuable in several applications. In medicine, it's been used to visualize the propagation of ultrasound waves in therapies and diagnostic tools, such as High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU). It provides a direct, real-time visualization of the ultrasound field, which can improve the precision and safety of these procedures. In engineering and physics, it's used to study heat transfer, gas flows, and shockwaves.

The fourth edition of Jonathan Riley-Smith’s book, What Were the Crusades?, published by the Ignatius Press on March 23, 2009, is a self-described introduction to the crusading movements of the medieval period. The book primarily covers the First through Fifth Crusades to the Middle East, issued by the Catholic Church, with the primary objective being to take Jerusalem and its surrounding territories. It also covers the French crusades, also known as King Louis IX’s first and second crusades, respectively. It finely details the reasoning, justification, planning, and execution of the crusades, as well as the sociopolitical consequences of the crusades in Europe and the Middle East.
What makes Riley-Smith’s work exemplary among others is how he challenged the generally accepted definition of the crusades. He states in his preface for the third edition that the widely accepted yet baseless tenets of the field, prior to his studies, were as follows: “True” crusading was defined as attempts from Europe to gain control of Jerusalem; the crusaders’ opponents in the Middle East were culturally superior to them; most of them departed in hopes of gaining land, money, and political power; the military orders were religious orders in name only; and the Crusader states were a colonial experiment.
What Were the Crusades? serves as an academic rebuttal of these viewpoints, namely the first, third, and fourth points, as the second and fifth points were no longer considered worthy of serious discussion. Riley-Smith argues that crusading was not just limited to expeditions to the Middle East, but was done across Europe for centuries; the Crusades were in fact a religious war for the vast majority of those who took the cross; and the military orders were as much of a religious order as any other division of the church. These claims are presented not in tandem with but as a result of Riley-Smith’s goal of the book, which is to define the “who, what, where, and why” of the Crusades using concrete evidence rather than unfounded claims.
Naturally, Riley-Smith opens with a broad but satisfactory definition of the crusades — a series of religious and political expeditions aimed at reclaiming, defending, and conquering lands deemed important to Christianity. These military campaigns were usually initiated and supported by the Catholic Church, with the first crusade correctly taking place in 1095 by the decree of Pope Urban II. It finely details the reasoning, justification, planning, and execution of the crusades, as well as the sociopolitical consequences of the crusades in Europe and the Middle East.
What makes Riley-Smith’s work exemplary among others is how he challenged the generally accepted definition of the crusades. He states in his preface for the third edition that the widely accepted yet baseless tenets of the field, prior to his studies, were as follows: “True” crusading was defined as attempts from Europe to gain control of Jerusalem; the crusaders’ opponents in the Middle East were culturally superior to them; most of them departed in hopes of gaining land, money, and political power; the military orders were religious orders in name only; and the Crusader states were a colonial experiment.
What Were the Crusades? serves as an academic rebuttal of these viewpoints, namely the first, third, and fourth points, as the second and fifth points were no longer considered worthy of serious discussion. Riley-Smith argues that crusading was not just limited to expeditions to the Middle East, but was done across Europe for centuries; the Crusades were in fact a religious war for the vast majority of those who took the cross; and the military orders were as much of a religious order as any other division of the church. These claims are presented not in tandem with but as a result of Riley-Smith’s goal of the book, which is to define the “who, what, where, and why” of the Crusades using concrete evidence rather than unfounded claims.

Eurocentrism- East and West: the two binaries
Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Consequently, Eurocentric discourse breeds a false dichotomy between the West and non-European societies, perpetuating the notion that the West is superior and in control of all areas of life, including social, political, cultural, scientific, military, and economic fields. Disparaging epithets are often attributed to the “non-West,” reinforcing connotations of inferiority, irrationality, belligerence, otherness, fanaticism, and barbarism in comparison to the West. This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. This belief in Western superiority is often reinforced through various forms of discourse, including history, literature, art, music, etc. In a similar vein, through the utilization of Eurocentric and imperialistic perspectives, academic discourse has consistently depicted ‘Eastern societies’ as exotic and racialized, perpetuating a biased portrayal of the Orient or East. In his seminal text Orientalism (1979), Edward Said, a Palestinian critic, asserts that “European culture gained in strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self.” (3) This dichotomy between the West and the East often presents the West as a modern, flowing territory and the East as a static, archaic region. Therefore, the Orient functions as a mirror to the West in that the West relies heavily on its counterpart, the Orient, for its own sense of superiority. (Sandy and Ouardi, 2019, p. 129) On the other hand, this discourse of exoticism, essentialism, and stereotyping of the East and its people has been used to justify colonization, exploitation, and violence against Eastern civilizations.
